content: Ohio University, established in 1804, is the oldest higher education institution in Ohio and the first in the Northwest Territory. It is located on a 3-square-kilometer campus in Athens, strategically chosen for its position between Chillicothe, the original capital of Ohio, and Marietta. Initially named American Western University, it was founded a year after Ohio joined the Union. The Northwest Ordinance of 1800 emphasized the importance of education for good governance and societal happiness, encouraging the establishment of schools and educational institutions. In 1797, settlers from Marietta traveled up the Hocking River to identify a suitable location for the university, ultimately selecting Athens. Ohio University is renowned for its academic programs, including the Scripps School of Journalism, established with a grant from the Scripps Foundation, and the College of Osteopathic Medicine, which opened in 1975 and remains the only osteopathic college in Ohio. The university is also recognized for its Avionics Engineering Center, part of the Russ College of Engineering, specializing in research and development of electronic navigation, communication, and surveillance systems. The John Calhoun Baker Center, a $65 million student center, opened in January 2007. It features Georgian-style architecture, expansive windows, and a contemporary interior design with ergonomic furniture and a welcoming color scheme. The six-story facility includes a food court, fine dining restaurant, ballroom, coffee shop, theater, computer labs, and office spaces, connected by escalators that create a mall-like atmosphere. This design earned recognition as a best practice by the Association of College Unions International in 2006. Ohio University is organized into several colleges, including Arts & Sciences, Business, Communication, Education, Engineering, Fine Arts, Health & Human Services, Honors Tutorial College, University College, Osteopathic Medicine, and the Center for International Studies. It also operates five regional campuses in Eastern (St. Clairsville), Zanesville, Lancaster, Southern (Ironton), and Chillicothe. The university is classified as a Doctoral/High Research Activity institution by the Carnegie Foundation, reflecting its expanding graduate programs. It is one of several public universities in Ohio with this classification, alongside Bowling Green State University, Kent State University, Miami University, the University of Akron, the University of Toledo, and Wright State University. Ohio University students have achieved notable success in securing nationally competitive awards, including Fulbright Scholarships, Mitchell Scholarships, Truman Scholarships, Udall Scholarships, Goldwater Scholarships, and Hollings Scholarships. In 2006, twelve students received Fulbright Scholarships, and in 2005, nine students were awarded the same honor. The university fosters a robust research environment, hosting various research programs and institutes. These include the Institute for Sustainable Energy and the Environment, the Center for Advanced Materials Processing, the Avionics Engineering Research Center, and the Institute for Corrosion & Multiphase Technology, among others. The College of Arts and Sciences sponsors institutes such as the African American Research and Service Institute and the Astrophysical Institute. The College of Osteopathic Medicine supports the Interdisciplinary Institute for Neuromusculoskeletal Medicine and the Tropical and Geographical Disease Institute. Ohio University is also home to the Kennedy Museum of Art, which houses significant collections of Native American textiles, jewelry, and contemporary prints. The museum offers exhibitions, educational programs, and tours. The School of Recreation and Sport Sciences is nationally recognized, offering undergraduate and graduate programs in athletic training, exercise physiology, physical education, recreation studies, and sport management. Its Sport Management Program is one of approximately thirty in the country approved by the Sport Management Program Review Council. The Russ College of Engineering and Technology, named after alumnus Dr. Fritz J. Russ, enrolls around 1,400 undergraduates and 300 graduate students. It offers programs in traditional engineering fields and is known for its contributions to bioengineering. Ohio University's athletic teams, known as the Bobcats, compete in NCAA Division I as part of the Mid-American Conference (MAC). The football program, established in 1894, has a storied history, including five MAC Football Championships and a National Small College Championship in 1960. The men's basketball program has won five MAC Tournament titles and participated in the NCAA Tournament eleven times. The university's volleyball, swimming, diving, wrestling, and baseball teams have also achieved significant success. The university's athletic facilities, including Peden Stadium and the Convocation Center, are among the best in the MAC and the nation. The Marching 110 band, known for its high-energy performances, has performed at prestigious events, including Carnegie Hall and the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Ohio University operates public FM radio stations under the Ohio University Public Radio umbrella and a PBS-affiliated public television station, WOUB. The university's student-run radio station, ACRN, features a rock lobster mascot and broadcasts exclusively online. The WOUB Center for Public Media produces Wired for Books, recognized as one of the best online educational resources in the humanities. Ohio University boasts a distinguished list of alumni, including Roger Ailes, Richard Dean Anderson, Bob Brenly, Nancy Cartwright, Matt Lauer, and Mike Schmidt, among others. These individuals have excelled in various fields, including media, sports, arts, and public service.
